title: Isaiah 39:1–8
context: At that time Merodach-baladan sent letters and a present to Hezekiah; Hezekiah showed them all his treasure house; Isaiah asks what they said; days are coming when all that is in your house will be carried to Babylon; Hezekiah: the word of the LORD is good, there will be peace and security in my days. The unit stays with that historic Babylonian embassy, 8th/7th century—as Wesley and Calvin actually read—not a newspaper, not a millennial camp fight.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Merodach-baladan’s letters and present, Hezekiah showing the treasure house, Isaiah asking what they said, the days coming when all that is in the house will be carried to Babylon, and Hezekiah saying the word of the LORD is good, there will be peace and security in his days—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 39:1–8.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The king of Babylon sends ambassadors with letters and a present to Hezekiah, who shews them his treasures, ver. 1, 2. Isaiah foretells the Babylonish captivity, ver. 4-7. His resignation, ver. 8. Berodach-baladan—He seems to have been the king of Assyria’s vice-roy in Babylon, and upon that terrible slaughter in the Assyrian host, and the death of Sennacherib, and the differences among his sons, to have usurped absolute sovereignty over Babylon. And either himself or his son destroyed the Assyrian monarchy, and translated the empire to Babylon. Sent—Partly, for the reasons mentioned, 2 Chron. 32:31, and partly, to assure himself of the assistance of Hezekiah against the Assyrians, their common enemy. Shewed—Which he did through pride of heart, 2 Chron. 32:25, 26, being lifted up by the great honour which God had done him, in working such glorious miracles for his sake, and by the great respects rendered to him from divers princes, and now by this great Babylonian monarch. So hard a matter is it even for a good man to be high and humble. Behold—This judgment is denounced against him for his pride; for his ingratitude, whereby he took that honour to himself which he should have given entirely to God; and for his carnal confidence in that league which he had now made with the king of Babylon, by which, it is probable, he thought his mountain to be so strong, that it could not be removed. Thy sons—Of thy grand-children. Eunuchs—They shall be servants to that heathen monarch, whereby both their bodies will be subject to slavery, and their souls exposed to the peril of idolatry, and all sorts of wickedness. Good is, &c.—I heartily submit to this sentence, as being both just, and merciful. True penitents, when they are under divine rebukes, call them not only just, but good. Not only submit to, but accept of the punishment of their iniquity. So Hezekiah did, and by this it appeared, he was indeed humbled for the pride of his heart.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 39:1–8; 2 Kgs 20:12–19)

reformed.quote: At that time. Some think that this was the first king of the Chaldee nation; for his father, Baladin, had held the government over the Babylonians without the title of king. This Merodach, therefore, after having reigned twelve years, subdued the Assyrians, and made them tributaries to the Chaldeans; for it is a mistake to suppose that the war was begun by Nebuchadnezzar. Sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: this was done craftily by the Babylonian, in order to flatter and cajole Hezekiah; the pretence was, to congratulate Hezekiah on having recovered from his disease; yet sacred history appears to assign another reason, which was, that Merodach was induced by a miracle; the mind of the good king was corrupted by ambition, so that he too eagerly accepted the false blandishments of the tyrant, and swallowed the bait. And Hezekiah was glad: blinded by ambition, he made an ostentatious display to the messengers; there lurked in his heart a desire of vain ostentation; he directed his mind to foreign and unlawful aid, and to that extent denied honor to God, whom he had recently known to be his deliverer on two occasions. This is a remarkable example; nothing is more dangerous than to be blinded by prosperity; it is more difficult to bear prosperity than adversity. Then came Isaiah the Prophet: he did not come as a private individual; he was not sent for, but came though he was not invited; in adversity the prophets are sought, but in prosperity are disregarded. What did those men say? he does not immediately inflict a severe reproof, but wounds him gently, so as to lead him to a confession of his sin. Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah: from this judgment we perceive that the sin of Hezekiah was not small; God observes in Hezekiah’s joy, first, ingratitude; next, pride; the chief fault was ambition. Behold, the days come: he takes from his successors those things of which he vaunted so loudly; the Lord punishes the ambition and pride of men. Of thy sons: it might be thought that this was far more distressing to Hezekiah, and therefore it is put last; when he understood that his sons would be made captives and slaves, this must have appeared to him to be exceedingly severe. Good is the word of Jehovah: Hezekiah was not a stubborn or obstinately haughty man; when he is informed that the Lord is angry, he unhesitatingly acknowledges his guilt; he does not argue or contend with the Prophet, but conducts himself with gentleness and modesty. At least there shall be peace: the particle ki here denotes an exception, and therefore I have translated it at least; Hezekiah gives thanks to God for mitigating the punishment which he had deserved; it is more probable that what the Prophet had said about the days that were to come, Hezekiah applied for soothing his grief, to encourage himself to patience. It might be thought that Hezekiah was cruel in taking no care about posterity; but he does not disregard posterity; perceiving that God moderates the punishment by forbearance, he gives thanks to God.

verses.text: At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: The king of Babylon sends ambassadors with letters and a present to Hezekiah, who shews them his treasures, ver. 1, 2. Berodach-baladan—He seems to have been the king of Assyria’s vice-roy in Babylon, and upon that terrible slaughter in the Assyrian host, and the death of Sennacherib, and the differences among his sons, to have usurped absolute sovereignty over Babylon. And either himself or his son destroyed the Assyrian monarchy, and translated the empire to Babylon. Sent—Partly, for the reasons mentioned, 2 Chron. 32:31, and partly, to assure himself of the assistance of Hezekiah against the Assyrians, their common enemy.

Arminian reading: they might yet have received those letters and that present from that king of Babylon, not a later chart. Historic Babylonian embassy, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another Merodach to make “letters and a present” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: at that time. Some think that this was the first king of the Chaldee nation; for his father, Baladin, had held the government over the Babylonians without the title of king. This Merodach, therefore, after having reigned twelve years, subdued the Assyrians, and made them tributaries to the Chaldeans; for it is a mistake to suppose that the war was begun by Nebuchadnezzar. Sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: this was done craftily by the Babylonian, in order to flatter and cajole Hezekiah; the pretence was, to congratulate Hezekiah on having recovered from his disease; yet sacred history appears to assign another reason, which was, that Merodach was induced by a miracle.

Reformed note: the letters and the present stay that historic embassy to this king. Calvin will not let Merodach-baladan become a newspaper of later courts.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep Merodach-baladan as that historic king of Babylon who sent the embassy, not a newspaper and not a millennial camp fight. Wesley reads him as the king of Assyria’s vice-roy in Babylon who, after the slaughter in the Assyrian host and the death of Sennacherib, usurped absolute sovereignty over Babylon; either himself or his son destroyed the Assyrian monarchy and translated the empire to Babylon. Calvin takes him as the first king of the Chaldee nation: his father Baladin had held the government without the title of king; this Merodach, after having reigned twelve years, subdued the Assyrians and made them tributaries to the Chaldeans; it is a mistake to suppose that the war was begun by Nebuchadnezzar. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight. Neither makes the embassy a later headline.

verses.text: And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Shewed—Which he did through pride of heart, 2 Chron. 32:25, 26, being lifted up by the great honour which God had done him, in working such glorious miracles for his sake, and by the great respects rendered to him from divers princes, and now by this great Babylonian monarch. So hard a matter is it even for a good man to be high and humble. His treasures—For though his country had lately been harassed by the Assyrians, yet he had reserved all his treasures and precious things, which he and his fathers had gathered in Jerusalem.

Arminian reading: they might yet have shown that treasure house through pride of heart, not a later chart. Historic showing of this king, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another storehouse to make “he showed them his treasure house” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: and Hezekiah was glad. Blinded by ambition, he made an ostentatious display to the messengers; there lurked in his heart a desire of vain ostentation; he wished to make a favorable display of himself, that the Babylonian might be led to understand that this alliance would not be without advantage to him. He deserved to be reproved on another ground, that he directed his mind to foreign and unlawful aid, and to that extent denied honor to God, whom he had recently known to be his deliverer on two occasions. This is a remarkable example; nothing is more dangerous than to be blinded by prosperity.

Reformed note: the treasure house stays that historic showing of this king. Calvin will not let the silver and the gold become a newspaper of later vaults.

verses.text: Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, “What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?” Hezekiah said, “They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: The king of Babylon sends ambassadors with letters and a present to Hezekiah, who shews them his treasures, ver. 1, 2—still that embassy when Isaiah the prophet came to king Hezekiah, and said, What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee? And Hezekiah said, They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have answered that they came from a far country, from Babylon, not a later chart. Historic question of this prophet, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another far country to make “what did these men say” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: then came Isaiah the Prophet. He did not come as a private individual; he was not sent for, but came though he was not invited; in adversity the prophets are sought, but in prosperity are disregarded. What did those men say? he does not immediately inflict a severe reproof, but wounds him gently, so as to lead him to a confession of his sin. And yet it is evident from the reply that Hezekiah was not yet struck by that gentle reproof; he boasts that those men came from a distant country, from Babylon, because he was under the influence of ambition.

Reformed accent: Isaiah’s coming stays that historic question to this king. Calvin will not let “from a far country, from Babylon” become a newspaper of later envoys.

verses.text: He said, “What have they seen in your house?” Hezekiah answered, “They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: The king of Babylon sends ambassadors with letters and a present to Hezekiah, who shews them his treasures, ver. 1, 2—still that showing when he said, What have they seen in thine house? And Hezekiah answered, All that is in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.

Arminian reading: they might yet have answered that they had seen all that was in the house, not a later chart. Historic confession of this king, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another house to make “what have they seen in your house” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: then he said. Isaiah proceeds in his indirect admonition, to see if Hezekiah shall be moved by it and displeased with himself. He does not break out against the Prophet, but modestly confesses the state of the fact, though he does not yet acknowledge that he has sinned. Ambition deludes men so much, that by its sweetness it not only intoxicates but drives them mad, so that, even when they have been admonished, they do not immediately repent.

Reformed note: what they have seen stays that historic confession of this king. Calvin will not let the storehouses become a newspaper of later inventories.

verses.text: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of hosts:
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Isaiah foretells the Babylonish captivity, ver. 4-7—still that word when Isaiah said to Hezekiah, Hear the word of the LORD of hosts.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have heard that word of the LORD of hosts, not a later chart. Historic word to this king, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another host to make “hear the word of the LORD of hosts” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: then Isaiah said to Hezekiah. From this judgment of God we perceive that the sin of Hezekiah was not small; God observes in Hezekiah’s joy, first, ingratitude; next, pride; the chief fault was ambition. Hear the word of Jehovah of hosts: being about to be the bearer of a harsh sentence, he begins by saying that he is God’s herald; he does not dread the face of the king, or fear to make known his disease, and to announce to him the judgment of God.

Reformed accent: “hear the word” stays that historic sentence to this king. Calvin will not let the LORD of hosts become a newspaper of later courts.

verses.text: Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Behold—This judgment is denounced against him for his pride; for his ingratitude, whereby he took that honour to himself which he should have given entirely to God; and for his carnal confidence in that league which he had now made with the king of Babylon, by which, it is probable, he thought his mountain to be so strong, that it could not be removed. Isaiah foretells the Babylonish captivity, ver. 4-7—still that carrying to Babylon of all that is in the house.

Arminian reading: they might yet have heard that the days are coming when all that is in the house shall be carried to Babylon, not a later chart. Historic captivity named upon this embassy, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another Babylon to make “nothing shall be left” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: behold, the days come. He takes from his successors those things of which he vaunted so loudly, in order that they may have no ground for boasting of them. Thus the Lord punishes the ambition and pride of men, so that their name or kingdom, which they hoped would last for ever, is blotted out. If it be objected that it is unreasonable that the sacking of a city and the captivity of a nation should be attributed to the fault of a single man, there is no absurdity in God’s punishing the sin of a single man, and at the same time the crimes of a whole nation.

Reformed note: the carrying to Babylon stays that historic word against this house. Calvin will not let “nothing shall be left” become a newspaper of later loot.

verses.text: And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Thy sons—Of thy grand-children. Eunuchs—They shall be servants to that heathen monarch, whereby both their bodies will be subject to slavery, and their souls exposed to the peril of idolatry, and all sorts of wickedness. Isaiah foretells the Babylonish captivity, ver. 4-7—still those sons taken away after the house of v. 6.

Arminian reading: they might yet have named those sons as grand-children made eunuchs in that palace, not a later chart. Historic sons of this house, 8th/7th century, are already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another palace to make “they shall be eunuchs” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: of thy sons. It might be thought that this was far more distressing to Hezekiah, and therefore it is put last for the sake of heightening the picture. Even though any calamity spread widely in a nation, it is commonly thought that kings and their families will be exempted. When he understood, therefore, that his sons would be made captives and slaves, this must have appeared to him to be exceedingly severe. Hence again we may learn how much God was displeased with Hezekiah for seeking aid from earthly wealth, and boasting of it in the presence of wicked men.

Reformed note: the sons stay those historic captives of this house. Calvin will not let the eunuchs become a newspaper of later palaces.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the sons as those historic captives of this house, not a newspaper and not a millennial camp fight. Wesley reads “thy sons” as of thy grand-children; they shall be eunuchs, servants to that heathen monarch, whereby both their bodies will be subject to slavery, and their souls exposed to the peril of idolatry and all sorts of wickedness. Calvin takes the sons as put last for the sake of heightening the picture, far more distressing to Hezekiah: when he understood that his sons would be made captives and slaves, this must have appeared to him exceedingly severe; kings and their families are not exempt. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight. Neither makes the eunuchs a later headline.

verses.text: Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “There will be peace and security in my days.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: His resignation, ver. 8. Good is, &c.—I heartily submit to this sentence, as being both just, and merciful. True penitents, when they are under divine rebukes, call them not only just, but good. Not only submit to, but accept of the punishment of their iniquity. So Hezekiah did, and by this it appeared, he was indeed humbled for the pride of his heart.

Arminian close of the unit: they might yet have called that word good and owned peace in his days, not a later chart. Historic resignation of this king, 8th/7th century, is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another peace to make “there will be peace and security in my days” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: good is the word of Jehovah. Hezekiah was not a stubborn or obstinately haughty man; when he is informed that the Lord is angry, he unhesitatingly acknowledges his guilt; he does not argue or contend with the Prophet, but conducts himself with gentleness and modesty. At least there shall be peace: the particle ki here denotes an exception, and therefore I have translated it at least; Hezekiah gives thanks to God for mitigating the punishment which he had deserved. It might be thought that Hezekiah was cruel in taking no care about posterity; but he does not disregard posterity; perceiving that God moderates the punishment by forbearance, he gives thanks to God, and bears more patiently the calamity which was to come.

Reformed close: “the word of the LORD is good” stays that historic resignation of this king. Calvin will not let “peace and security in my days” become a newspaper of later truces.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep Hezekiah’s word as that historic resignation after the embassy, not a newspaper and not a millennial camp fight. Wesley reads “Good is the word” as hearty submission, both just and merciful: true penitents, when they are under divine rebukes, call them not only just, but good; they not only submit to, but accept of the punishment of their iniquity; so Hezekiah did, and by this it appeared he was indeed humbled for the pride of his heart. Calvin also finds genuine submissiveness, yet he translates ki as “at least”: Hezekiah gives thanks for mitigating the punishment; some think him cruel in taking no care about posterity, but he does not disregard posterity—he applies the days that were to come for soothing his grief, and thanks God that the promise of his own days is ratified. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight. Neither makes “peace and security in my days” a later headline.
